A quick note before we dive in: I've intentionally omitted a deep dive into Israel's role and its "Greater Israel" agendas in this analysis. Not because it's unimportant, far from it, but because the situation is widely understood, and this post focuses specifically on the overlooked economic and supply chain dynamics involving China, the US, and their allies.

After starting a fire, 𝐃𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥𝐝 𝐓𝐫𝐮𝐦𝐩 is now asking the world for a fire extinguisher. Let that sink in.

The man who boasted about "𝑑𝑒𝑠𝑡𝑟𝑜𝑦𝑖𝑛𝑔 100% 𝑜𝘧 𝐼𝑟𝑎𝑛'𝑠 𝑚𝑖𝑙𝑖𝑡𝑎𝑟𝑦 𝑐𝑎𝑝𝑎𝑏𝑖𝑙𝑖𝑡𝑦" is now on Truth Social, practically sending out invitations to China, France, Japan, South Korea, and the UK, pleading for warships in the Strait of Hormuz.

If you "destroyed" everything, Mr. President, why do you need the entire planet to come save your shipping lanes?

Here is what nobody is saying loudly enough.

This war was never just about Iran. It was always about the ghost at the table: Beijing.

China purchases roughly 80% of Iran's oil exports. The two nations share a $400 billion, 25-year Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. Chinese radar systems, navigation technology, and missile components have quietly strengthened Iran's electronic warfare capabilities throughout this conflict. Russia has been feeding Iran real-time intelligence on American warship positions using satellite data.

And yet, Trump has the audacity to ask China to send warships alongside America to reopen a strait that America's own war closed.

Beijing's response was telling. A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington told CNN that China wants an immediate cessation of hostilities and that "𝑎𝑙𝑙 𝑝𝑎𝑟𝑡𝑖𝑒𝑠 𝘩𝑎𝑣𝑒 𝑡𝘩𝑒 𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑝𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑖𝑏𝑖𝑙𝑖𝑡𝑦 𝑡𝑜 𝑒𝑛𝑠𝑢𝑟𝑒 𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑏𝑙𝑒 𝑎𝑛𝑑 𝑢𝑛𝑖𝑚𝑝𝑒𝑑𝑒𝑑 𝑒𝑛𝑒𝑟𝑔𝑦 𝑠𝑢𝑝𝑝𝑙𝑦." Translation: you broke it, you fix it, we will watch.

Iran told the IRGC to let Chinese ships pass through Hormuz. It told the Americans they would be targeted. That is not the behaviour of a "totally decapitated" nation. That is a nation with a very powerful friend watching from the wings.

Notice something interesting? Trump struck military sites on Kharg Island (the source of 90% of Iran's oil exports) but deliberately spared the oil infrastructure, citing "𝑟𝑒𝑎𝑠𝑜𝑛𝑠 𝑜𝘧 𝑑𝑒𝑐𝑒𝑛𝑐𝑦."

Decency has nothing to do with it.

The real calculation is China. Destroying Iran's oil infrastructure would be a direct assault on Beijing's energy security. Roughly 13% of China's total seaborne crude intake flows from Iran. It would cross the invisible red line that separates a Middle Eastern military operation from a great power confrontation.

And here is the leverage Washington truly fears. China controls roughly 70% of global rare earth production and dominates processing even more completely. Beijing has already banned rare earth exports for military use. An F-35 fighter jet carries 435 kilograms of rare earths. Every precision-guided missile, every advanced radar system, every drone the US is using in this campaign depends on materials that flow through Chinese hands.

Reports from the South China Morning Post suggest Washington holds approximately two months of rare earth inventory. Two months. China could, without firing a single bullet, determine how long America can sustain this war simply by tightening a supply chain.

When Trump threatened 100% tariffs last year, China's answer was simple: no more processed rare earths. Trump backed down immediately. That tells you everything about who holds the real power in this equation.

The Carnegie Endowment put it precisely: Western analysts expect China to behave like the United States, and when China does not, they call it failure rather than recognising it as a deliberate choice. Beijing does not rescue regimes. Beijing diversifies portfolios. It plays markets, not battlefields. And right now, with America burning through weapons, goodwill, and strategic credibility in the Persian Gulf, China is quietly positioning itself as the stable, peaceful alternative for every nation in the Global South watching this unfold.

The numbers do not lie.

Oil prices have surged 40% since this war began. Brent crude has touched $126 per barrel, the highest in four years. The Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed. Over 150 ships sit stranded. Tanker traffic dropped to near zero. Gulf energy infrastructure is being hit by Iranian drones. The UAE's Fujairah port was struck and forced to suspend operations. Qatar halted LNG production, knocking out 20% of global LNG exports. The Formula 1 races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia have been cancelled. Six American air crew died when a KC-135 refuelling aircraft crashed in Iraq.

Goldman Sachs has raised US recession odds to 25%. Oxford Economics warns that oil at $140 per barrel would push the Eurozone, the UK, and Japan into economic contraction. Fertiliser prices have skyrocketed from $475 to $680 per metric ton ahead of America's planting season. Bangladesh is closing universities early. Pakistan and the Philippines have declared four-day work weeks. India has invoked emergency powers to protect 333 million LPG-dependent households.

𝐴𝑛𝑑 𝑇𝑟𝑢𝑚𝑝'𝑠 𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑝𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑒? "𝐼𝑡 𝑑𝑜𝑒𝑠𝑛'𝑡 𝑟𝑒𝑎𝑙𝑙𝑦 𝑎𝘧𝘧𝑒𝑐𝑡 𝑢𝑠."

Meanwhile, China is playing the long game with surgical precision. It is stockpiling oil reserves (estimated at 120 days of supply), receiving discounted crude from Iran and Russia through shadow fleets, positioning itself as the "peaceful superpower" to the Global South, and quietly preparing to dictate the terms of the next global order from its seat at the rare earth table.

The IRGC Navy chief said it best: "Americans falsely claimed the destruction of Iran's navy. Then they falsely claimed the escorting of oil tankers. Now they are even asking others for backup forces."

𝑇𝘩𝑒 𝑛𝑒𝑡 𝑘𝑒𝑒𝑝𝑠 𝑤𝑖𝑑𝑒𝑛𝑖𝑛𝑔. It is no longer just about the countries Trump named on Truth Social. 𝐁𝐨𝐭𝐡 𝐖𝐚𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐭𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐓𝐞𝐥 𝐀𝐯𝐢𝐯 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐜𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐠𝐥𝐨𝐛𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐩 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐠𝐦𝐢𝐫𝐞, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐀𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐚 𝐡𝐚𝐬 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐛𝐞𝐞𝐧 𝐬𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐝.

On 10 March, the Albanese government announced the deployment of 85 personnel, a Boeing E-7A Wedgetail surveillance aircraft, and stocks of air-to-air missiles to the United Arab Emirates. The Prime Minister insists this is "defensive" and that Australia will not deploy ground troops to Iran. But let us be honest about how these things unfold.

France is already preparing a "purely defensive" escort mission for ships through the Strait of Hormuz, and analysts have warned that Australia could be asked to join that effort next. The Greens leader, Larissa Waters, was blunt: this is Australia being drawn into another "US-led forever war." She pointed out that Trump and Netanyahu's demands of Australia keep growing. It was refuelling US spy planes yesterday, a reconnaissance jet and missiles today, and could be ever more troops tomorrow.

She is not wrong.

We watched the same pattern with Afghanistan. We watched it with Iraq in 2003. It begins with "surveillance assets" and "defensive missiles." Then the mission scope expands. Then the casualties begin. Then two decades later, we ask ourselves how we got there. Australia lost 41 soldiers in Afghanistan. The Iraq war cost us credibility, resources, and moral standing on the world stage. And now we are walking towards the same door again, one "limited deployment" at a time.

Australia, Canada, Germany, Finland, New Zealand, and over a dozen other nations have now expressed at least partial support for the US-Israeli strikes. Iran's security commission warned from the very first day that it would drag every country in the region into war. The irony is that Washington and Tel Aviv are doing precisely the same thing; they are just calling it "coalition building."

Given that Australia's own oil supplies and fuel costs are directly impacted by the closure of the Strait, the government would find it difficult to say no if asked for more. That is the trap. You start a war without consulting your allies, you destabilise the world's most critical energy chokepoint, and then you tell nations like Australia that they have a "responsibility" to help clean up the mess.

As an Australian who has called this country home, I find it deeply troubling that our nation keeps finding itself at the doorstep of conflicts we did not start, fighting for objectives that are not ours, at the behest of powers that did not ask our opinion before lighting the match.

America started a war without a plan for the world's most important energy chokepoint. It "destroyed" Iran's military but cannot reopen a 21-mile wide waterway. It is now begging the nations it has alienated, sanctioned, and lectured for decades to come clean up the mess. It has dragged its allies, including Australia, into a conflict that a CNN poll shows 60% of Americans themselves disapprove of.

Welcome to Trump's Wonderland.

Where you declare total victory on social media while the real world burns. Where you ask your adversary's closest partner to join your coalition. Where the country you cannot name in polite strategic conversation (China) holds the actual keys to whether your war machine keeps running. And where nations like Australia, on the other side of the planet, are quietly being pulled into a fire they had no hand in starting.

The 21st century will not be defined by who drops the most bombs. It will be defined by who controls the supply chains, the energy corridors, and the rare earth minerals that make modern warfare possible.

On that scoreboard, America is not winning.

It is not even close.

Agree? 

Disagree? 

The conversation matters more than the opinion.
